            *model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_8_max-online-service-deployment*
ONLINE SERVICE DEPLOYMENT

         *model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_8_max-multi-node-online-deployment*
Multi-node online deployment

Multi-node deployment distributes the model across multiple A3 Series nodes
using tensor parallelism while keeping prefill and decode on the same nodes
(PD mixed mode), suitable for scenarios that need more device memory than a
single node can provide. The validated configuration deploys the W4A8
quantized checkpoint on 4 nodes with `--tp-size 64` (16 dies per node), DP
attention (`--attn-dp-size 4`), and DeepEP in `auto` mode.

Modify the IP addresses of the four nodes, then run the same script on all
four nodes. Each node determines its own rank by matching the local IP
address against `IPS`.

>sh
    # ============================================================
    # Before running, update the following variables:
    #   IPS: IP addresses of each node in the cluster
    #   MODEL_PATH: path to the model weights directory
    #   HCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME: network interface name for HCCL
    #   GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME: network interface name for Gloo
    # ============================================================

    # high performance cpu
    echo performance | tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor
    sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10
    sysctl -w kernel.numa_balancing=0
    sysctl -w kernel.sched_migration_cost_ns=50000
    # bind cpu
    export SGLANG_SET_CPU_AFFINITY=1
    export SGLANG_ONE_VISIBLE_DEVICE_PER_PROCESS=1

    unset https_proxy
    unset http_proxy
    unset HTTPS_PROXY
    unset HTTP_PROXY
    unset ASCEND_LAUNCH_BLOCKING
    # cann
    source /usr/local/Ascend/ascend-toolkit/set_env.sh
    source /usr/local/Ascend/nnal/atb/set_env.sh

    export PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True
    export STREAMS_PER_DEVICE=32

    # deepep
    export DEEP_NORMAL_MODE_USE_INT8_QUANT=1
    export SGLANG_DEEPEP_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK=128
    export HCCL_BUFFSIZE=2300
    export DEEPEP_NORMAL_LONG_SEQ_ROUND=64
    export DEEPEP_NORMAL_LONG_SEQ_PER_ROUND_TOKENS=512
    export HCCL_OP_EXPANSION_MODE=AIV

    # Run command ifconfig on each node, find out which inet addr has same IP with your node IP. That is your public interface, which should be added here
    export HCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=<network-interface>
    export GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=<network-interface>

    IPS=('<your node1 ip>' '<your node2 ip>' '<your node3 ip>' '<your node4 ip>')
    IP_MASTER="${IPS[0]}:5000"

    MODEL_PATH=/path/to/model-weights

    LOCAL_HOST1=`hostname -I|awk -F " " '{print$1}'`
    LOCAL_HOST2=`hostname -I|awk -F " " '{print$2}'`
    for i in "${!IPS[@]}";
    do
        if [[ "$LOCAL_HOST1" == "${IPS[$i]}" || "$LOCAL_HOST2" == "${IPS[$i]}" ]];
        then
            echo "${IPS[$i]}"

            # overlap schedule
            export SGLANG_ENABLE_OVERLAP_PLAN_STREAM=1
            export SGLANG_RAGGED_VERIFY_MODE=static

            sglang serve \
                --model-loader-extra-config '{"enable_multithread_load": true}' \
                --dist-init-addr $IP_MASTER --nnodes 4 --node-rank $i \
                --model-path $MODEL_PATH \
                --tokenizer-path $MODEL_PATH \
                --trust-remote-code \
                --attention-backend ascend \
                --device npu \
                --quantization modelslim \
                --dtype bfloat16 \
                --tp-size 64 \
                --attn-dp-size 4 --enable-dp-lm-head \
                --mem-fraction-static 0.8 \
                --chunked-prefill-size 8192 \
                --cuda-graph-bs-decode 16 \
                --disable-radix-cache \
                --max-running-requests 64 \
                --host 0.0.0.0 \
                --port 30000 \
                --moe-a2a-backend deepep \
                --deepep-mode auto \
                --watchdog-timeout 9000
            break
        fi
    done
<

Qwen3-8B                          *sglang-model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_8b*

INTRODUCTION                *model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_8b-introduction*

Qwen3-8B is a compact dense model in the Qwen3 series developed by Alibaba,
featuring 8B parameters with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and up to 128k
context length. It delivers significant improvements in instruction
following, logical reasoning, text comprehension, mathematics, science,
coding, and tool usage. The model supports EAGLE3 speculative decoding for
accelerated inference and is available in both standard and
thinking/reasoning-enhanced editions.

This document demonstrates the deployment of Qwen3-8B on Ascend NPUs using
SGLang, including single-node PD mixed mode, feature configuration, and
performance optimization.

The commands in this document use the daily build image
`quay.io/ascend/sglang:main-cann9.1.0-a3`.

SUPPORTED FEATURES    *model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_8b-supported-features*

Feature               Example usage
--------------------  --------------------------------------------------------
Tensor Parallelism    --tp-size 2
Quantization          --quantization modelslim
Chunked Prefill       auto based on device memory, or set explicit
                      value;disable with --chunked-prefill-size -1; e.g.,
                      --chunked-prefill-size 8192
NPU Graph             enabled by default; disable with
                      --disable-decode-cuda-graph
                      --disable-prefill-cuda-graph;control range via
                      --cuda-graph-bs-decode or --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode;
                      e.g., --cuda-graph-bs-decode 1 2 4 6 9 10 15 16
Speculative Decoding  --speculative-algorithm EAGLE3
                      \--speculative-draft-model-path
                      /path/to/draft-model-weights \--speculative-num-steps 3
                      \--speculative-eagle-topk 1
                      \--speculative-num-draft-tokens 4
                      \--speculative-draft-model-quantization unquant
Overlap Schedule      export SGLANG_ENABLE_OVERLAP_PLAN_STREAM=1

  Note: ~

  The values in the Example usage column are for illustration only. Adjust
  them according to your hardware, deployment mode, and workload. For
  parameter details, see
  |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parameter-reference|; for
  recommended configurations for each deployment scenario, see
  |model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_8b-best-practices|.

For feature compatibility and conflict information between features, see
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-feature-compatibility|.

Model weights              *model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_8b-model-weights*

- Qwen3-8B-W8A8 https://www.modelscope.cn/models/vllm-ascend/Qwen3-8B-w8a8
  (W8A8 quantized version, 11.27GB)

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    docker pull quay.io/ascend/sglang:main-cann9.1.0-a3

    docker run -itd --shm-size=16g --name ${NAME} \
    --privileged=true --net=host \
    -v /var/queue_schedule:/var/queue_schedule \
    -v /etc/ascend_install.info:/etc/ascend_install.info \
    -v /usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/sbin \
    -v /usr/local/Ascend/driver:/usr/local/Ascend/driver \
    -v /usr/local/Ascend/firmware:/usr/local/Ascend/firmware \
    --device=/dev/davinci0:/dev/davinci0  \
    --device=/dev/davinci1:/dev/davinci1  \
    --device=/dev/davinci2:/dev/davinci2  \
    --device=/dev/davinci3:/dev/davinci3  \
    --device=/dev/davinci4:/dev/davinci4  \
    --device=/dev/davinci5:/dev/davinci5  \
    --device=/dev/davinci6:/dev/davinci6  \
    --device=/dev/davinci7:/dev/davinci7  \
    --device=/dev/davinci8:/dev/davinci8  \
    --device=/dev/davinci9:/dev/davinci9  \
    --device=/dev/davinci10:/dev/davinci10  \
    --device=/dev/davinci11:/dev/davinci11  \
    --device=/dev/davinci12:/dev/davinci12  \
    --device=/dev/davinci13:/dev/davinci13  \
    --device=/dev/davinci14:/dev/davinci14  \
    --device=/dev/davinci15:/dev/davinci15  \
    --device=/dev/davinci_manager:/dev/davinci_manager \
    --device=/dev/hisi_hdc:/dev/hisi_hdc \

  Tip: ~

FUNCTIONAL VERIFICATION

After the service is started, you can invoke the model by sending a prompt:

>sh
    # ============================================================
    # Before running, update the following variables:
    #   HOST: the server host address (e.g., localhost)
    #   PORT: the server port number (e.g., 6688)
    # ============================================================

    curl http://${HOST}:${PORT}/generate \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{
            "text": "What is the capital of France?",
            "sampling_params": {
                "max_new_tokens": 64,
                "temperature": 0
            }
        }'
<
Expected result: an HTTP 200 response with the generated text containing
“Paris”.

               *sglang-model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_next_80b_a3b_instruct*
Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct

         *model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_next_80b_a3b_instruct-introduction*
INTRODUCTION

Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct is a hybrid Gated DeltaNet-Transformer
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model developed by Alibaba, featuring 80B total
parameters with 3B active parameters. It combines Gated DeltaNet SSM layers
with attention layers in a sparse MoE architecture, enabling efficient
long-sequence modeling with linear complexity in the SSM layers. The model
supports multi-token prediction (NEXTN) for speculative decoding, delivering
strong performance in instruction following, reasoning, and text generation
tasks.

This document demonstrates the deployment of Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct on
Ascend NPUs using SGLang, including single-node PD mixed mode, feature
configuration, and performance optimization.

The commands in this document use the daily build image
`quay.io/ascend/sglang:main-cann9.1.0-a3`.

   *model-deployment-tutorials-qwen3_next_80b_a3b_instruct-supported-features*
SUPPORTED FEATURES

Feature               Example usage
--------------------  --------------------------------------------------------
Tensor Parallelism    --tp-size 4
Data Parallelism      --dp-size 2
Expert Parallelism    --ep-size 4 \--moe-a2a-backend deepep \--deepep-mode
                      auto
Quantization          --quantization modelslim
NPU Graph             enabled by default; disable with
                      --disable-decode-cuda-graph
                      --disable-prefill-cuda-graph;control range via
                      --cuda-graph-bs-decode or --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode;
                      e.g., --cuda-graph-bs-decode 2 4 8
Speculative Decoding  --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \--speculative-num-steps 3
                      \--speculative-eagle-topk 1
                      \--speculative-num-draft-tokens 4
                      \--speculative-draft-model-quantization unquant
                      \--speculative-draft-model-path
                      /path/to/draft-model-weights
Overlap Schedule      export SGLANG_ENABLE_OVERLAP_PLAN_STREAM=1
DP LM Head            --enable-dp-lm-head

  Note: ~

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Parameter Tuning            *sglang-ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning*

This page assumes a server that already runs. It answers two questions:
which parameter to change for a goal, and what each parameter does and costs
on Ascend. Full launch scripts, multi-node topology, and the settings a
deployment shape requires --- the PD roles, the KV-transfer backend and
rendezvous store, the network interfaces --- belong to the per-model Best
Practices pages.

Which script you start from decides how much of this page you need. With a
best-practice page for your model, adopt its script as the baseline: most of
the batch checklist is already set, so the work reduces to diffing the
script and moving the one knob your workload needs. Without one, start from
a minimal launch (see the Model Tutorials
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/hardware-platforms/ascend-npus/model-deployment/tutorials
index) and build up with the same workflow --- switches first, then knobs.

|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-how-to-tune| is the workflow.
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parameter-reference| is the
complete inventory, one row per parameter.
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-tuning-by-goal| says where to
start for a goal, and
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-feature-compatibility| checks a
combination before you launch it.

  Note: ~

  Flag names and values change across releases: the best-practice pages pin
  the scripts of the image they were validated on, while this page tracks
  current builds. If a flag here is rejected or has no effect on your build,
  trace how the name evolved in the repository --- an AI assistant pointed
  at the codebase is a fast way --- and check
  |sglang-ascend-npus-reference-support_features| for per-flag support
  status.

HOW TO TUNE            *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-how-to-tune*

1
Measure a baseline

Pick the target metric --- TTFT, TPOT, throughput, or memory headroom ---
and benchmark the current configuration before changing anything. Record the
seed, input/output lengths, and concurrency with every run.

Follow one measurement protocol across runs: flush the prefix cache, keep
warmup identical, repeat the same benchmark a few times to learn its noise
floor, and treat any difference inside that spread as noise rather than a
win. |sglang-ascend-npus-evaluation-performance_testing| has the command and
how to read Mean TTFT/Mean TPOT; |sglang-ascend-npus-optimization-profiling|
gives a kernel-level view.

2
Batch-enable the add-on switches

Add every switch from the
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batch-checklist| whose Applies
when matches your model and role. If you started from a best-practice
script, diff the list against it and add only what is missing.

3
Verify the batch in three checks, in order

1. The server starts.
2. The |sglang-ascend-npus-evaluation-accuracy_evaluation| passes ---
   mandatory after speculative decoding.
3. The benchmark improves or holds.

If a check fails, remove the added switches one at a time; nearly every
failure is a precondition violation stated in that switch's row.

4
Tune the knobs top-down, one at a time

Fix the topology first --- parallelism, PD disaggregation, and the
communication buffers that go with them --- then the load-shape parameters
that consume memory
(|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|,
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|,
speculative depth), and size
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory| last,
because activation and graph buffers come out of the same budget.

Choices at one level bound what the levels below can reach: graph-level
tuning cannot compensate for a wrong TP/EP split. Re-measure after every
change, keep the better configuration, record every configuration you
benchmark so the results stay comparable, and keep the previous one so you
can roll back.

Batch checklist    *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batch-checklist*

The switches to add in step 2, each linking to its section in
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parameter-reference|:

Switch                                Applies when
------------------------------------  ----------------------------------------
SGLANG_NPU_USE_MLAPO=1                DeepSeek-style MLA
SGLANG_USE_FIA_NZ=1                   DeepSeek-style MLA
SGLANG_NPU_USE_MULTI_STREAM=1         MoE models with shared experts --- the
                                      DeepSeek, GLM, Qwen-MoE, and LongCat
                                      code paths all read it
SGLANG_USE_AG_AFTER_QLORA=1 +         Model with q_lora_rank; practically
--enable-attn-tp-input-scattered      prefill-only
SGLANG_ENABLE_OVERLAP_PLAN_STREAM=1   Speculative decoding on, no LoRA
--enable-dp-lm-head                   Attention DP on
PYTORCH_NPU_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True  Always
Host OS settings: governor            Always (commands run as root)
performance, vm.swappiness=0,
kernel.numa_balancing=0,
kernel.sched_migration_cost_ns=50000
SGLANG_SET_CPU_AFFINITY=1             Always
Speculative decoding                  Model ships an MTP head (NEXTN), or you
                                      supply an external draft model (EAGLE3);
                                      verify accuracy after enabling

  Tip: ~

  Fusion and stream-overlap switches are the largest unconditional wins on
  MoE models. Allocator and host settings are smaller but apply to every
  deployment. Speculative decoding is the single largest lever, but only
  while acceptance holds.

To match the Applies when column against your model, read its `config.json`:
MLA models carry `kv_lora_rank` (with `q_lora_rank` additionally gating the
gather-after-Q switch), MoE models with shared experts carry
`n_shared_experts`, and a NextN/MTP head appears as
`num_nextn_predict_layers`. |sglang-ascend-npus-reference-support_models|
lists the validated model families, and each model's best-practice page
shows which of these switches its script sets.

The remaining switches are conditional --- also on/off, but the payoff
depends on the workload, so they are not part of the batch. Enable one only
when evidence from benchmarks, metrics, or the traffic shape says its
condition holds; the condition and the failure are in the row's trade-offs.

Conditional switch                  Enable when
----------------------------------  ------------------------------------------
SGLANG_SCHEDULER_SKIP_ALL_GATHER=1  DP load is balanced --- uneven load desyncs
                                    silently
--enable-eplb                       Expert-load metrics show imbalance
--disable-radix-cache               Requests share no prefixes
--deepep-dispatcher-output-dtype    Prefill dispatch traffic dominates ---
int8 /                              typically multi-node; the accuracy budget
DEEP_NORMAL_MODE_USE_INT8_QUANT=1   allows a small loss
TASK_QUEUE_ENABLE=2                 The role captures no graphs
HCCL_OP_EXPANSION_MODE=AIV          Never on Atlas A2 systems with DeepEP

               *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parameter-reference*
PARAMETER REFERENCE

Every tuning parameter on Ascend, in five groups. Unless a row says
otherwise, the Reference value comes from the published DeepSeek V3.2 PD
configuration on 32 NPUs: a starting point from that validated deployment,
not a flag default. On a single mixed node there are no roles to split ---
start from the raw defaults and let
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-tuning-by-goal| drive the
changes.

  Tip: ~

  Three shapes, three readings. Range rows give what raising and lowering
  buys, with the failure mode at each end. Discrete rows give the valid
  values and the pick. Switch rows give the condition to enable, and the
  cost of enabling it anyway.

Reading the tables. `—` means do not set the flag. A trailing parenthetical
narrows when a value applies: a model list, as in `1` (DeepSeek R1), or a
condition, as in `on (long-context prefill)`. Raw defaults for most flags
are in |sglang-ascend-npus-reference-support_features|, and most environment
variables in |sglang-ascend-npus-reference-environment_variables|.

Two groups are omitted, and both are copied from your model's best-practice
script rather than tuned here. Setup settings have nothing to size, and a
wrong rank or an unreachable interface hangs startup: `HCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME` /
`GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME`, `--nnodes`, `--node-rank`, `--dist-init-addr`. The
other group is what those scripts pin per model, hardware series, or build:
the `ZBAL_*` / `ZBCCL_*` KV-transfer switches, `ASCEND_USE_FIA`,
`GDN_ATTN_BACKEND_TRITON`, the DeepSeek V4 `SGLANG_OPT_*` group, and the
speculative-decoding switches they set (`SGLANG_ENABLE_SPEC_V2`,
`SGLANG_SPEC_ENABLE_OVERLAP_REFLOW`, `FORCE_DRAFT_MODEL_NON_QUANT`).

        *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-graph-batch-size-alignment*
Graph batch-size alignment

Decode buckets are filtered against a batch-size alignment. The alignment is
`attn_tp_size` whenever a gathered buffer is in use --- attention DP, any
MoE all-to-all backend, or an explicit `--moe-dense-tp-size` --- and `1`
otherwise. Two-batch overlap (two micro-batches per step, planned on Ascend;
see |sglang-ascend-npus-reference-support_features| for availability on your
build) doubles the alignment, and context parallelism can raise it further.
A bucket survives when batch size × per-request decode tokens is a multiple
of the alignment; with speculative decoding the draft tokens already supply
part of that multiple, so buckets below the alignment can survive. Buckets
that miss the alignment are dropped, and startup aborts if none survive.

In practice, set
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory| to at
least the alignment and to a multiple of it whenever attention DP, an
all-to-all backend, or `--moe-dense-tp-size` is in play. A dense model with
plain TP has no such constraint.

Two defaults follow from this area. NPU prefill graphs are off by default,
so no prefill graph flag is needed. And to disable only decode graphs on a
mixed node, use `--disable-decode-cuda-graph`. The published prefill scripts
pass `--disable-decode-cuda-graph --disable-prefill-cuda-graph`; on a
dedicated prefill role that captures no graphs this is redundant and
harmless.

 *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-sizing-the-deepep-dispatch-buffer*
Sizing the DeepEP dispatch buffer

Size
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-moe-dispatch-and-communication|
to the maximum number of tokens one rank dispatches per decode iteration:
running requests per rank × `--speculative-num-draft-tokens` with
speculative decoding, or just the running requests per rank without it.

The published value `8` leaves headroom over its benchmark load: 8
concurrent requests over DP 8 is one request per rank, which is `1 × 4 = 4`
dispatched tokens per iteration, half the buffer. Serving the full
`--max-running-requests 32` cap would need `(32 / 8) × 4 = 16`, so raise the
value when you serve more concurrency than the benchmark did.

The default is `128` when unset. DeepEP enforces a hard cap of `1024`, but
the `ascend_fuseep` path bypasses that check and, with its default
`--fuseep-mode 2`, treats the variable as received-token capacity instead
--- the DeepEP formula does not carry over.

TUNING BY GOAL      *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-tuning-by-goal*

Where to start for common goals, ordered by expected impact. Each goal is a
thin index into
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parameter-reference|: the entries
name the parameters with the largest expected effect, and the full
constraint and failure modes live in each row's trade-offs. Turn on every
applicable switch from the
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batch-checklist| first, and check
the enable condition of any workload-dependent switch you add.

Almost every parameter moves more than one goal, directly or indirectly. A
smaller prefill chunk buys TTFT and costs prefill throughput; a higher graph
batch cap buys throughput and costs memory. So no goal can list every
parameter that acts on it: each list below is a starting point, not a closed
set. Expect a change made for one goal to move the others, and expect knobs
listed under one goal to move another.

For a target held under a budget on another metric --- output throughput
within a TPOT cap, say --- sweep the knob that sets the budget first, pin it
where the constrained metric sits just inside its bound, and only then sweep
the maximizing knob.

         *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-lower-decode-latency-tpot*
Lower decode latency (TPOT)

On MLA and DeepSeek-style MoE models, enable the MLAPO and multistream-MoE
switches from the
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batch-checklist| first; the knobs
below come after them.

1. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-speculative-decoding-and-quantization|
   (`--speculative-num-steps`, `--speculative-num-draft-tokens`) --- one
   target forward verifies several draft tokens. Watch the `accept len:` /
   `accept rate:` fields: acceptance drifts with output content, and at very
   high concurrency the verification overhead can cost throughput instead.
2. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   --- remove kernel-launch overhead.
3. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| --- more
   independent decode instances.
4. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| --- further
   reduction, only with balanced DP load.
5. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   --- on mixed workloads with attention DP, bounded prefill delays keep
   decode fed when it would otherwise stall behind prefill bursts (it pays
   TTFT for TPOT).

Cross-goal. The delayer pays TTFT, a higher graph cap costs memory, and
verification spends compute that high concurrency cannot repay --- the
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-lower-time-to-first-token-ttft|,
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-resolve-out-of-memory-errors|,
and |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-higher-throughput| goals read
these knobs from the other side.

                 *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-higher-throughput*
Higher throughput

1. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| --- more
   independent decode instances.
2. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   --- more concurrent requests per node.
3. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-model-specific-switches-and-host|
   --- parallelize tokenization across worker processes.
4. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   --- more KV cache, while monitoring for out-of-memory errors.

Check the load supply before sizing server-side knobs. Client concurrency,
`--max-running-requests`, and the batch the server actually forms are three
different numbers: requests above the capacity cap only queue, and the
effective batch is what the `Decode batch` lines report per rank. Sweep
client concurrency against a fixed server configuration first; once the
server saturates, more concurrency buys queueing and TTFT, not throughput.

Cross-goal. More concurrency raises TPOT, and the memory fraction that buys
KV is the same budget the
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-resolve-out-of-memory-errors|
goal spends.

    *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-lower-time-to-first-token-ttft*
Lower time to first token (TTFT)

1. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory| on
   mixed workloads --- short requests are not delayed behind a single long
   prefill.
2. Prefix caching --- leave
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   unset, so shared prompt prefixes reuse KV.
3. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| for long inputs
   --- one sequence split across devices.

Cross-goal. A smaller chunk interleaves more fairly but lowers prefill
throughput, and context parallelism adds inter-device traffic --- the
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-higher-throughput| and
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-lower-decode-latency-tpot| goals
read the same knobs from the other side.

      *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-resolve-out-of-memory-errors*
Resolve out-of-memory errors

Decide first whether the hardware can hold the model at all: get the
checkpoint's total size from its download page, or run `du -sh` on the
weights directory, and compare it against your total device memory. If the
cards and machines should hold the weights with room to spare, the shortage
is in the memory budget rather than the hardware.

1. Lower
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   --- leave room for activations and graph buffers, at less KV cache and
   fewer concurrent requests.
2. Add
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   --- mitigates the allocator fragmentation that drives out-of-memory
   errors on MoE-scale models.
3. Load a
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-speculative-decoding-and-quantization|
   checkpoint --- W8/W4 weights cut weight memory by approximately 50%/75%,
   at a small accuracy loss.
4. Scale out --- a wider
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| or
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism|.

If startup instead fails with
`Not enough memory … increase --mem-fraction-static`, the KV pool is too
small: see |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-troubleshooting|.

Cross-goal. KV headroom is taken from concurrency, quantization from
accuracy, and a wider TP from all-reduce bandwidth --- every fix here is a
cost booked under another goal.

               *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-serve-long-contexts*
Serve long contexts

1. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| +
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| +
   |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parallelism| --- shard one
   sequence's KV and attention across devices.
2. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory|
   --- let concurrent long requests co-batch in one forward.
3. |ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory| on
   a dedicated prefill group --- the entire sequence prefilled in one pass.

Cross-goal. Context parallelism adds inter-device traffic, and an unchunked
prefill keeps decode waiting wherever the two share a node --- long-context
settings are the most likely to shift
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-lower-decode-latency-tpot|.

          *ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-from-an-observed-symptom*
From an observed symptom

The goals above start from what you want; this table starts from what you
see on a running deployment. Utilization and communication shares come from
|sglang-ascend-npus-optimization-profiling|; batch numbers come from the
recurring `Decode batch` log line --- `#running-req:` per rank, or
`sglang:num_running_reqs` on `/metrics`. Because the goals are coupled, a
symptom usually points at a knob filed under a different goal --- follow the
row, not the section.

----------------------------------  ------------------------------------------

                                    gating (--min-free-slots-delay)

                                    --min-free-slots-delay)

                                    rows, prefix-cache distribution across DP
                                    ranks
Communication dominates while       Parallel granularity: --tp-size,
operators run small                 --moe-dense-tp-size, --enable-dp-lm-head ---
                                    confirm with a profile first

                                    and graph capture range --- see Resolve
                                    out-of-memory errors
Throughput improved but TTFT        Queueing and admission delay --- the
worsened                            trade-off the change was expected to pay.
                                    Re-read the row of the knob you moved.

*ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-tune-a-pd-disaggregated-or-multi-node-deployment*
Tune a PD-disaggregated or multi-node deployment

PD disaggregation itself is a deployment decision rather than a knob: the
role flags, the KV-transfer backend, the rendezvous store, the bootstrap
port, and the router belong to setup, and the per-model best-practice page
owns them (for DeepSeek V3.2, see the
|sglang-model-deployment-best-practices-deepseek_v3_2|). Under
disaggregation every row of
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-parameter-reference| can take a
different value per role; the published V3.2 configuration splits them like
this:

The roles differ because their workloads differ: prefill is throughput-bound
on large token counts (bulk dispatch buffers, un-chunked batches, no graphs
worth capturing), while decode is latency-bound (small graph-captured
batches, the low-latency dispatch path, deeper speculation). Both roles load
the same ModelSlim W8A8 checkpoint; only the budget each leaves for KV cache
differs, which is why their memory fractions differ. Decode also sets
`SGLANG_ENABLE_OVERLAP_PLAN_STREAM=1` and
`SGLANG_SCHEDULER_SKIP_ALL_GATHER=1`, whose preconditions are in their rows.

Roles also differ in knobs this configuration does not set: published
prefill roles tune the DeepEP long-sequence dispatch pipeline and shrink
`HCCL_BUFFSIZE` (see
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-moe-dispatch-and-communication|),
and several models add
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-batching-graphs-and-memory| ---
those rows carry the per-role values.

For a multi-node deployment that is not disaggregated, the extra knobs are
the communication ones ---
|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-moe-dispatch-and-communication|
and INT8 dispatch on prefill
(|ascend-npus-optimization-parameter_tuning-moe-dispatch-and-communication|).

conflict, not a guarantee. For per-flag support status, see
|sglang-ascend-npus-reference-support_features|.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------
Performance Profiling              *sglang-ascend-npus-optimization-profiling*

During inference serving, it is sometimes necessary to monitor the internal
execution flow of the serving framework to identify performance issues. By
collecting start/end timestamps of key flows, identifying critical functions
or iterations, recording key events, and gathering relevant information, you
can quickly locate performance bottlenecks.

This guide walks you through the complete workflow of collecting performance
data in an SGLang Ascend NPU inference service --- from preparation,
collection, and analysis to visualization --- helping you get started with
performance profiling quickly.

For more profiling scenarios (e.g., Nsight Systems, PD disaggregation,
etc.), see SGLang Benchmark and Profiling
https://docs.sglang.io/docs/developer_guide/benchmark_and_profiling.

                  *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-ascend-pytorch-profiler*
ASCEND PYTORCH PROFILER

SGLang has built-in PyTorch Profiler support. Through the Ascend `torch_npu`
backend, you can directly collect NPU operator-level performance data. No
additional packages are required --- profiling start/stop is controlled via
API requests.

1. Environment Setup  *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-1-environment-setup*

Launch an SGLang online service and set the `SGLANG_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR`
environment variable to control where performance files are saved. Once the
service starts, profiling is ready on standby.

  Note: ~

  `/start_profile` and `/stop_profile` are admin endpoints: the server must
  be launched with `SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY` set (or `--admin-api-key`), and
  each request must carry that key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. Without
  an admin key configured, the server answers HTTP 403. The examples below
  assume the key is exported as `SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY`.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # Set the performance data output directory
    export SGLANG_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR=./sglang_profile
    export SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY=<key>

    # Start SGLang server (use local model path or HuggingFace model id)
    sglang serve \
      --model-path /path/to/your/model \
      --attention-backend ascend \
      --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
      --tp-size 1 \
      --max-running-requests 128
<
Profiling-related environment variables:

Variable                      Description                              Default
----------------------------  ---------------------------------------  -------
SGLANG_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR     Trace file output directory              /tmp
SGLANG_PROFILE_WITH_STACK     Record Python call stack (True / False)  True
SGLANG_PROFILE_RECORD_SHAPES  Record operator input shapes (True /     True
                              False)

  Note: ~

  Priority order: API parameter > Environment variable > Default value.

                     *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-2-collection-methods*
2. Collection Methods

SGLang provides four collection methods. The core differences are whether
you need to manually send `/start_profile` and `/stop_profile`. All four
methods produce identical results --- choose the most convenient one.

Method comparison:

Method              Manual              Manual              Notes
                    start_profile       stop_profile
------------------  ------------------  ------------------  ------------------
A: API manual       Yes                 Yes                 Maximum
start/stop                                                  flexibility for
                                                            precise control
B: API auto-stop    Yes                 No                  Set num_steps,
                                                            auto-stops and
                                                            generates output
C: bench_serving    No                  No                  Benchmark +
---profile                                                    profiling in one
                                                            command
D: sglang.profiler  No                  No                  Standalone
CLI                                                         profiling CLI tool

           *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-method-a-api-manual-start/stop*
Method A: API Manual Start/Stop

Send `/start_profile` to start → send workload requests → send
`/stop_profile` to stop. After stopping, the server automatically parses the
data --- no need to manually call `analyse()`.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # Step 1: Start profiling (no num_steps, requires manual stop)
    curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30000/start_profile \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY}" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{
        "output_dir": "./sglang_profile",
        "start_step": 1,
        "activities": ["CPU", "GPU"]
      }'

    # Step 2: Send workload requests (using curl as example)
    curl http://127.0.0.1:30000/generate \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"text": "Hello", "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 10}}'

    # Step 3: Stop profiling
    curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30000/stop_profile \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY}"
<
  Note: ~

  `/stop_profile` returns `"Stop profiling. This will take some time."` ---
  the server needs time to flush trace data to disk and parse it. Wait for
  the response to complete. This method takes a significant amount of time
  to parse profiling data; consider using Method B instead to avoid lengthy
  waits.

                   *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-method-b-api-auto-stop*
Method B: API Auto-Stop

Specify `num_steps` in the `/start_profile` request. Profiling stops
automatically after N steps and generates output --- no need to manually
send `/stop_profile`.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # num_steps=10, wait 3 warmup steps, auto-stop after 10 steps
    curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30000/start_profile \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer ${SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY}" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{
        "output_dir": "./sglang_profile",
        "start_step": 3,
        "num_steps": 10,
        "activities": ["CPU", "GPU"]
      }'

    # Just send workload — no /stop_profile needed
    curl http://127.0.0.1:30000/generate \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"text": "Hello", "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 32}}'
<

           *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-method-c-bench_serving-profile*
Method C: bench_serving ---profile

Use SGLang's built-in `bench_serving` with the `--profile` flag.
Automatically handles `/start_profile` and `/stop_profile` --- no manual API
calls needed.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # With --profile-steps: auto-stops after N steps and generates output
    python -m sglang.benchmark.serving \
      --backend sglang \
      --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
      --model /path/to/your/model \
      --tokenizer /path/to/your/model \
      --dataset-name random \
      --random-input-len 1024 \
      --random-output-len 100 \
      --num-prompts 10 \
      --profile \
      --profile-steps 10 \
      --profile-output-dir ./sglang_profile

    # Without --profile-steps: /stop_profile sent automatically after benchmark
    python -m sglang.benchmark.serving \
      --backend sglang \
      --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
      --model /path/to/your/model \
      --tokenizer /path/to/your/model \
      --dataset-name random \
      --random-input-len 1024 \
      --random-output-len 100 \
      --num-prompts 10 \
      --profile \
      --profile-output-dir ./sglang_profile
<
  Note: ~

  `--profile-steps N` sends `"num_steps": N` to the server's
  `/start_profile`, so the server auto-stops and parses data after N steps
  --- bench_serving skips sending `/stop_profile`.

  Note: ~

  `bench_serving --profile` creates a timestamp subdirectory inside
  `--profile-output-dir` (e.g., `<output_dir>/<timestamp>/`). The output
  path is shown in the server log as
  `Profiling done. Traces are saved to: <path>`.

  Note: ~

  On Ascend NPU, SGLang uses `torch_npu._apply_patches()` to automatically
  redirect PyTorch Profiler's CUDA activity to NPU, so
  `activities: ["CPU", "GPU"]` actually captures NPU operator events.

`bench_serving --profile` parameters:

Parameter            Description
-------------------  ---------------------------------------------------------
---profile             Enable auto profiling start/stop
---admin-api-key       The server's admin API key, required by ---profile
                     (default: SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY)
---profile-steps N     Auto-stop after N steps (skips /stop_profile)
---profile-output-dir  Trace output directory

             *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-method-d-sglang-profiler-cli*
Method D: sglang.profiler CLI

Use the `sglang.profiler` CLI module, which automatically sends
`/start_profile` and waits for completion. Start `sglang.profiler` first,
then send inference requests (otherwise there are no steps to capture and
the profiler will wait indefinitely).

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # Terminal 1: Start sglang.profiler first (sends /start_profile, then waits for completion)
    python3 -m sglang.profiler \
      --url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
      --output-dir ./my_profiles \
      --num-steps 3 \
      --cpu --gpu &
<
[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # Terminal 2: Wait for "Waiting for N steps" output from Terminal 1, then send requests.
    # The profiler starts recording once /start_profile is received by the server.
    # Requests sent before the server receives /start_profile will not be captured.
    curl http://127.0.0.1:30000/generate \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"text": "Hello", "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 32}}'
<
A simpler and more reliable approach is to use `bench_serving --profile`,
which handles both steps automatically:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.benchmark.serving \
      --backend sglang \
      --base-url http://127.0.0.1:30000 \
      --model /path/to/your/model \
      --tokenizer /path/to/your/model \
      --dataset-name random \
      --random-input-len 128 \
      --random-output-len 32 \
      --num-prompts 10 \
      --profile \
      --profile-steps 3 \
      --profile-output-dir ./my_profiles
<
  Note: ~

  `sglang.profiler` is essentially a CLI wrapper around the `/start_profile`
  API. Advanced options like `--profile-by-stage` are also supported. On
  Ascend NPU, trace flushing is asynchronous and may take a while --- the
  CLI may occasionally block waiting for flush. If it times out, use Method
  B (API auto-stop) or Method C (bench_serving ---profile) instead.

`sglang.profiler` CLI parameters:

Parameter                  Description
-------------------------  ---------------------------------------------------
---url                       SGLang server address
---admin-api-key             The server's admin API key, required by
                           /start_profile (default: SGLANG_ADMIN_API_KEY)
---output-dir                Output directory (defaults to
                           SGLANG_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR)
---num-steps                 Number of steps to profile
---profile-by-stage          Profile prefill / decode stages separately
---profile-prefix            Trace filename prefix
---cpu / ---gpu / ---mem / ---rpd  Activity types to collect

               *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-3-full-parameter-reference*
3. Full Parameter Reference

All methods ultimately send a `/start_profile` request to the server. The
full set of supported parameters:

Parameter         Description                                   Default
----------------  --------------------------------------------  --------------
output_dir        Output directory. Falls back to               /tmp
                  SGLANG_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR or /tmp
num_steps         Number of steps. If set, profiling            None
                  auto-stops --- no /stop_profile needed
start_step        Step index to start profiling (inclusive),    0
                  for skipping warmup
activities        Activity types: CPU, GPU, MEM, RPD. On        [“CPU”, “GPU”]
                  Ascend NPU, only CPU and GPU are supported.
                  MEM depends on CUDA memory APIs and will be
                  silently ignored. RPD requires ROCm and will
                  cause an error.
profile_by_stage  Profile prefill and decode stages separately  false
with_stack        Record Python call stack. Also controllable   true
                  via SGLANG_PROFILE_WITH_STACK
record_shapes     Record operator input shapes. Also            true
                  controllable via
                  SGLANG_PROFILE_RECORD_SHAPES
profile_prefix    Prefix for trace filenames                    None
profile_stages    Stages to profile, e.g., [“prefill”,          None
                  “decode”]. Requires profile_by_stage

                   *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-4-finding-output-files*
4. Finding Output Files

The server log explicitly indicates where traces are saved. You can find
them via:

- When profiling starts: server log outputs
  `Profiling starts. Traces will be saved to: <path> (with profile id: <id>)`

>text
    [2026-05-19 13:23:15] Profiling starts. Traces will be saved to: /tmp/1779196995.6948605 (with profile id: 1779196995.6979997)
    [2026-05-19 13:23:15] [WARNING] [350443] profiler.py: Invalid parameter export_type: None, reset it to text.
    [2026-05-19 13:23:15] [WARNING] [350443] profiler.py: Invalid parameter export_type: None, reset it to text.
    [2026-05-19 13:23:15] INFO:     127.0.0.1:40714 - "POST /start_profile HTTP/1.1" 200 OK
<
- When profiling stops: server log outputs
  `Profiling done. Traces are saved to: <path>`

>text
    [2026-05-19 13:23:17] Stop profiling...
    [2026-05-19 13:23:17] [WARNING] [350443] profiler.py: Incorrect schedule: Stop profiler while current state is RECORD which may result in incomplete parsed data.
    [rank0]:[W519 13:23:17.084812760 compiler_depend.ts:3136] Warning: The indexFromRank 0 is not equal indexFromCurDevice 4 , which might be normal if the number of devices on your collective communication server is inconsistent.Otherwise, you need to check if the current device is correct when calling the interface.If it's incorrect, it might have introduced an error. (function operator())
    [2026-05-19 13:23:17] [INFO] [352725] profiler.py: Start parsing profiling data: /tmp/1779196995.6948605/localhost.localdomain_350443_20260519132315700_ascend_pt
    [2026-05-19 13:23:22] [INFO] [352734] profiler.py: CANN profiling data parsed in a total time of 0:00:04.022310
    [2026-05-19 13:23:32] [INFO] [352725] profiler.py: All profiling data parsed in a total time of 0:00:14.305669
    [2026-05-19 13:23:32] Profiling done. Traces are saved to: /tmp/1779196995.6948605
<
- CLI output: `sglang.profiler` outputs `Dump profiling traces to <path>`

>text
    Dump profiling traces to /tmp/1779243331.3219
    Waiting for 10 steps and the trace to be flushed.... (profile_by_stage=False)
<
The directory structure is
`<output_dir>/<hostname>_<pid>_<timestamp>_ascend_pt/`. When using Method C
(`bench_serving --profile`), a timestamp subdirectory is added:
`<output_dir>/<timestamp>/<hostname>_<pid>_<timestamp>_ascend_pt/`. Always
check the server log for the exact path:
`Profiling done. Traces are saved to: <path>`.

5. Viewing Results      *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-5-viewing-results*

After profiling stops (either `/stop_profile` returns or `num_steps`
auto-triggers), the server automatically parses the raw data. The
`ASCEND_PROFILER_OUTPUT` directory directly contains the following
visualization files --- no need to manually call `analyse()`:

File                          Description
----------------------------  ------------------------------------------------
trace_view.json               Chrome Tracing format. Open in MindStudio
                              Insight
analysis.db                   Database-format performance data
ascend_pytorch_profiler_0.db  Database-format performance data
kernel_details.csv            Kernel-level data
operator_details.csv          Operator-level data
step_trace_time.csv           Step trace timing data

  Note: ~

  `trace_view.json` can also be opened using Chrome's built-in
  `chrome://tracing` or Perfetto UI https://ui.perfetto.dev/.

  Note: ~

  In a multi-node deployment, each node generates its own trace files. To
  merge them into a single unified trace, set `"merge_profiles": true` in
  the `/start_profile` request. However, on Ascend NPU, the merge feature
  does not fully support the `*_ascend_pt` format --- merged results may be
  incomplete or incorrect. It is recommended to view `trace_view.json` on
  each node individually instead. For more details, see
  Benchmark and Profiling
  https://docs.sglang.io/docs/developer_guide/benchmark_and_profiling#profiler-trace-merger-for-distributed-traces.

           *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-6-re-parsing-raw-data-optional*
6. Re-parsing Raw Data (Optional)

If you need to re-parse existing data with different parameters, or if
profiling was interrupted and `ASCEND_PROFILER_OUTPUT` was not
auto-generated, use `torch_npu`'s `analyse()` tool:

>python
    from torch_npu.profiler.profiler import analyse
    analyse("./sglang_profile/<hostname>_*_ascend_pt/")
<
  Note: ~

  Normally no need to manually run `analyse()` --- the server already parses
  data automatically. Only use this for re-parsing or handling interrupted
  data. Running `analyse()` when ASCEND_PROFILER_OUTPUT already exists will
  overwrite the original directory. If the original data is still needed,
  back it up before running `analyse()`.

BEST PRACTICES             *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-best-practices*

Common Notes                 *ascend-npus-optimization-profiling-common-notes*

- Finding output: Check the server log for
  `Profiling starts. Traces will be saved to: <path>` and
  `Profiling done. Traces are saved to: <path>`, or `sglang.profiler` output
  for `Dump profiling traces to <path>`.
- Control trace file size: Reduce the number of requests and output length
  using `--num-prompts` and `--random-output-len` to avoid trace files too
  large for browsers.
- Warmup iterations: Set `start_step` to skip the first few warmup steps and
  capture performance data under steady state.
- Profile step count: Large values for `num_steps` or `--profile-steps` can
  lead to lengthy profiling data parsing times. Reduce these values
  appropriately when you only need a quick overview.
- CUDA Graph impact: To see the full Python call stack → operator mapping in
  traces, add `--disable-decode-cuda-graph --disable-prefill-cuda-graph`
  when starting the server. Note that this reduces decode performance ---
  only use during profiling. To analyze CUDA Graph capture specifically, use
  `--enable-profile-cuda-graph` --- traces are saved to
  `SGLANG_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR/graph_capture_profile/`.
- Multi-node deployment: In multi-node environments, performance data is
  distributed across nodes. On Ascend NPU, the `merge_profiles` feature has
  limited support --- check
  `*_ascend_pt/ASCEND_PROFILER_OUTPUT/trace_view.json` on each node
  individually. In PD disaggregation mode, prefill and decode workers must
  be profiled separately --- see Profile In PD Disaggregation Mode
  https://docs.sglang.io/docs/developer_guide/benchmark_and_profiling#profile-in-pd-disaggregation-mode.

Quantization on Ascend          *sglang-ascend-npus-optimization-quantization*

To load already quantized models, simply load the model weights and config.
Again, if the model has been quantized offline, there's no need to add
`--quantization` argument when starting the engine. The quantization method
will be automatically parsed from the downloaded
`quant_model_description.json` or `config.json` config.

SGLang supports mix-bits quantization (independently defines and loads each
layer depending on the type of quantification specified in the
`quant_model_description.json`). Advanced mix-bits for MoE
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/17361 in progress, will add
independent quantization determination for the w13 (up-gate) and w2 (down)
layers.

ModelSlim on Ascend support https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/14504

Usage Examples:

- Dense model (e.g., Qwen3-14B-Q4_K_M.gguf):

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path Qwen3-14B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --tp-size 2
<
- MoE model (e.g., Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf):

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path Qwen3-30B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --tp-size 2
<
  Implementation Notes:

  - GGUF weights are pre-dequantized to FP16/BF16 during model loading on
    CPU, then transferred to NPU for inference. This trades higher memory
    usage for faster runtime performance (no per-forward-pass dequantization
    overhead).
  - MoE layers use `npu_grouped_matmul` and `npu_moe_init_routing` /
    `npu_moe_finalize_routing` for high-performance expert computation.
  - TP (tensor parallelism) sharding is supported for both dense and MoE
    GGUF models.

MXFP8 for LLM dense models (e.g., Qwen3 / Qwen3.5):

LLM dense W8A8 MXFP8 Linear support on Ascend was added in PR #22352
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/22352. Requires 950PR/DT Series
or newer (`npu_dynamic_mx_quant` is not available on A2/A3 Series).

- Online MXFP8 quantization (BF16/FP16 weights → MXFP8 at load time):

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
        --quantization mxfp8 \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --tp-size 1
<
- Offline MXFP8 quantization (msmodelslim pre-quantized weights,
  `W8A8_MXFP8` scheme; no `--quantization` flag needed --- auto-detected
  from `quant_model_description.json`):

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path /path/to/Qwen3-8B-W8A8-MXFP8 \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --tp-size 1
<
  Implementation Notes:

  - Online path: `Fp8Config.get_quant_method()` dispatches to
    `NPUMXFP8LinearMethod`. Weights are quantized once at load via
    `npu_dynamic_mx_quant(weight, dst_type=torch_npu.float8_e4m3fn)` and
    pre-transposed to `[in, out]`; activations are per-token quantized at
    inference and matmul runs via
    `npu_quant_matmul(..., group_sizes=[1, 1, 32])` (block_size = 32).
  - Offline path: `ModelSlimMXFP8Scheme` loads `float8_e4m3fn` weights +
    `float8_e8m0fnu` block scales pre-exported by msmodelslim. Transpose is
    kept as a non-contiguous view (`.data` assignment) --- calling
    `.contiguous()` would physically reorder the pre-quantized layout and
    break the block-scale mapping.
  - MoE MXFP8 (FusedMoE) for LLMs is documented in MXFP8 for LLM MoE models
    below.

MXFP8 for LLM MoE models (e.g. Qwen3-30B-A3B / Qwen3.5 MoE):

LLM MoE W8A8 MXFP8 (FusedMoE) support builds on the dense MXFP8 path.
Requires 950PR/DT Series or newer --- the fused MoE MX kernels
(`npu_grouped_matmul_swiglu_quant_v2`, `npu_dynamic_mx_quant`) are only
available on the 950PR/DT Series.

- Online MXFP8 quantization (BF16/FP16 expert weights → MXFP8 at load time):

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B \
        --quantization mxfp8 \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --tp-size 1
<
- Offline MXFP8 quantization (msmodelslim pre-quantized weights,
  `W8A8_MXFP8` scheme). No `--quantization` flag is needed: the
  `quant_model_description.json` shipped with the checkpoint selects both
  the ModelSlim path and the scheme automatically.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path /path/to/Qwen3-30B-A3B-W8A8-MXFP8 \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --tp-size 1
<
  Implementation Notes:

  - Both paths share the per-gmm kernel `NPUMXFP8MoEMethod`
    (`hardware_backend/npu/quantization/moe_methods.py`), which tells online
    from offline by weight dtype. Expert weights and their e8m0 block scales
    are kept as non-contiguous transpose views --- calling `.contiguous()`
    would tank HBM bandwidth.
  - Online path: `Fp8Config.get_quant_method()` dispatches FusedMoE layers
    to `NPUMXFP8OnlineMoEMethod`, which subclasses
    `UnquantizedFusedMoEMethod` and overrides only `create_moe_runner` to
    swap in the MXFP8 kernels --- weight creation, weight post-processing
    and the forward pass are the unquantized Ascend ones. BF16 expert
    weights `w13`/`w2` are quantized once at load via
    `npu_dynamic_mx_quant(dst_type=torch.float8_e4m3fn)` (a 3D `[E, N, K]`
    input is accepted directly).
  - Offline path: `ModelSlimMXFP8MoEScheme` (one instance per weight group)
    loads `float8_e4m3fn` expert weights + uint8 (e8m0, exponent + 127)
    block scales. The scale is reshaped `[E, N, K/32] → [E, N, K/64, 2]`
    (contiguous pairing, matching `npu_dynamic_mx_quant`) then transposed.
  - Forward: the no-A2A (`none`) pre-permute runs
    `npu_moe_init_routing_v2(quant_mode=3)`, which fuses the per-token MX
    activation quant into routing (e4m3 payload + e8m0 block scale, reshaped
    to the pair-split layout). `AscendRunnerCore` then runs gmm1
    `npu_grouped_matmul_swiglu_quant_v2` (cumulative `group_list`; fuses
    gate/up + swiglu + requant, so no separate activation step) → gmm2
    `npu_grouped_matmul` (count `group_list`). The UE8M0 (`float8_e8m0fnu`)
    scale dtypes are passed explicitly; the e4m3 `x`/`weight` dtypes are
    left implicit.
  - Router gate: msmodelslim may also quantize `mlp.gate` (`W8A8_MXFP8`).
    The gate is a `ReplicatedLinear`, so its quantization must be
    description-driven: for the offline `modelslim` path the gate is passed
    the quant config and dequantized correctly; the online path keeps it in
    BF16. Loading a quantized gate as BF16 without its block scale scrambles
    routing and produces garbage output.
  - Where the activation quant happens depends on the transport. On the
    no-A2A (`none`) path it is fused into routing as described above. DeepEP
    has no MXFP8 dispatch dtype, so it keeps dispatching BF16 and gmm1
    quantizes the hidden states itself via `npu_dynamic_mx_quant` before the
    fused kernel --- the two paths reach the same gmm1 input. Only the
    no-A2A path has been validated end-to-end on the 950PR/DT Series.

MXFP4 W4A8 for LLM dense models (e.g., Qwen3 / Qwen3.5):

LLM dense W4A8 (MXFP4 4-bit weights + MXFP8 8-bit activations) Linear
support was added in PR #23650
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/23650. Requires 950PR/DT Series
or newer.

- Online W4A8 quantization (BF16/FP16 weights → MXFP4 at load time):

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
        --quantization mxfp_w4a8 \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --tp-size 1
<
- Offline W4A8 quantization (msmodelslim pre-quantized weights, `W4A8_MXFP`
  scheme; no `--quantization` flag needed --- auto-detected from
  `quant_model_description.json`).

  Implementation Notes:

  - Weights are packed FP4 (`float4_e2m1fn_x2`, two nibbles per byte) with a
    UE8M0 per-block shared exponent (block_size = 32); activations are
    per-token MXFP8. Matmul runs via
    `npu_quant_matmul(..., x2_dtype=torch_npu.float4_e2m1fn_x2, group_sizes=[0, 0, 32])`.
  - The packed-FP4 dtype passed to the NPU ops (`dst_type` / `x2_dtype` /
    `input_dtype`) must be resolved from `torch_npu.float4_e2m1fn_x2` (an
    int enum), not the `torch.float4_e2m1fn_x2` dtype object, which recent
    op-plugin builds reject.
  - Online and offline share the same kernel path and layout; they differ
    only in the weight source (RTN at load vs msmodelslim calibration).

ModelSlim W4A8 MXFP4 for LLM MoE models:

SGLang auto-detects offline ModelSlim `W4A8_MXFP` MoE checkpoints from
`quant_model_description.json`; do not pass `--quantization`. This path
requires 950PR/DT Series or newer.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    MODEL_PATH=/path/to/w4a8-mxfp4-moe-model
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path "$MODEL_PATH" \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --tp-size 1
<
  Implementation Notes:

  - ModelSlim supplies packed MXFP4 `w13` and `w2` expert weights with UE8M0
    block scales (block size 32).
  - Ascend TP and DeepEP dispatch activations as BF16; this path does not
    request MXFP8 dispatch. SGLang dynamically quantizes each expert input
    to MXFP8 immediately before grouped matmul.

MXFP4 W4A4 for LLM dense models (e.g. Qwen3 / Qwen3.5):

LLM dense W4A4 (MXFP4 4-bit weights + 4-bit activations) Linear support was
added in PR #23795 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/23795.
Requires 950PR/DT Series or newer --- the dual-level online path uses the
`DualLevelQuantBatchMatmul` op, which A2/A3 Series lack. On the Ascend NPU
backend `--quantization mxfp4` selects this W4A4 path (on GPU the same flag
selects the upstream OCP MXFP4 MoE config instead).

- Online W4A4 quantization (BF16/FP16 weights → dual-level MXFP4 at load
  time):

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
        --quantization mxfp4 \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --mem-fraction-static 0.8 --tp-size 1
<
- Offline W4A4 quantization (msmodelslim pre-quantized weights, `W4A4_MXFP4`
  scheme; no `--quantization` flag needed --- auto-detected from
  `quant_model_description.json`).

  Implementation Notes:

  - Online (`NPUDualLevelMXFP4LinearMethod`) uses dual-level MXFP4: both
    weights and activations are quantized with a fine FP8 (E4M3) L0 block
    scale plus a coarser L1 scale via `npu_dynamic_dual_level_mx_quant`, and
    the matmul runs via `npu_dual_level_quant_matmul` (weight in
    FRACTAL_NZ). Dual-level captures per-block dynamic range far better than
    a single UE8M0 (power-of-2) scale, which is what made an earlier
    single-level RTN online path degenerate (greedy decoding could loop
    without emitting EOS).
  - Offline (`ModelSlimMXFP4Scheme` →
    `NPUSingleLevelMXFP4OfflineLinearMethod`) is single-level: msmodelslim's
    `W4A4_MXFP4` checkpoint ships single-level UE8M0 block scales
    (block_size = 32), so the matmul runs via
    `npu_quant_matmul(..., x1_dtype=x2_dtype=torch_npu.float4_e2m1fn_x2, group_sizes=[1, 1, 32])`.
    The online and offline paths therefore use different matmul kernels ---
    they no longer share the matmul path.
  - As with W4A8, the packed-FP4 dtype passed to the NPU ops (`dst_type` /
    `x2_dtype`) must be resolved from `torch_npu.float4_e2m1fn_x2` (an int
    enum), not the `torch.float4_e2m1fn_x2` dtype object, which recent
    op-plugin builds reject.
  - Validated end-to-end on 950PR/DT Series hardware.

ModelSlim W4A4 MXFP4 for LLM MoE models:

SGLang auto-detects offline ModelSlim `W4A4_MXFP4` MoE checkpoints from
`quant_model_description.json`; do not pass `--quantization`. This path
requires 950PR/DT Series or newer.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    MODEL_PATH=/path/to/w4a4-mxfp4-moe-model
    python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
        --model-path "$MODEL_PATH" \
        --device npu --attention-backend ascend \
        --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
        --tp-size 1
<
  Implementation Notes:

  - ModelSlim supplies packed MXFP4 `w13` and `w2` expert weights with UE8M0
    block scales (block size 32).
  - Ascend TP and DeepEP dispatch activations as BF16; this path does not
    request MXFP4 dispatch. SGLang dynamically quantizes each expert input
    to MXFP4 immediately before grouped matmul.

*ascend-npus-optimization-quantization-diffusion-model-quantization-on-ascend-npu*
DIFFUSION MODEL QUANTIZATION ON ASCEND NPU

SGLang-Diffusion supports MXFP8 online and offline quantization for
diffusion models (such as Wan2.2) on Ascend NPUs. MXFP8 requires 950PR/DT
Series; the ModelSlim W8A8/W4A4 schemes work on A2/A3 Series.

Requirements for MXFP8: CANN ≥ 8.0.RC3, 950PR/DT Series

method        in JSON                                      Series     Series
                                                           Supported  Supported

             *ascend-npus-optimization-quantization-online-mxfp8-quantization*
Online MXFP8 Quantization

Online quantization dynamically quantizes FP16/BF16 weights to MXFP8 at load
time using `npu_dynamic_mx_quant` + `npu_quant_matmul` CANN kernels. Pass
`--quantization mxfp8` to override auto-detection.

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # Start the diffusion server with online MXFP8 quantization
    sglang serve \
      --model-path Wan-AI/Wan2.2-T2V-A14B-Diffusers \
      --quantization mxfp8 \
      --num-gpus 4
<
[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    # One-shot generation
    sglang generate \
      --model-path Wan-AI/Wan2.2-T2V-A14B-Diffusers \
      --quantization mxfp8 \
      --prompt "a beautiful sunset over the mountains" \
      --save-output
<

  *ascend-npus-optimization-quantization-offline-mxfp8-quantization-modelslim*
Offline MXFP8 Quantization (ModelSlim)

For offline quantization, pre-quantize the model with msModelSlim and load
the resulting checkpoint. The quantization scheme is auto-detected from
`quant_model_description.json`, so no extra `--quantization` flag is needed.

Step 1: Quantize with msModelSlim

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    msmodelslim quant \
      --model_path /path/to/wan2_2_float_weights \
      --save_path /path/to/wan2_2_mxfp8_weights \
      --device npu \
      --model_type Wan2_2 \
      --quant_type mxfp8 \
      --trust_remote_code True
<
  Note: SGLang does not support quantized embeddings; disable embedding
  quantization when using msmodelslim.

Step 2: Convert to Diffusers format

msModelSlim saves quantized Wan2.2 weights in the original Wan format.
Convert to Diffusers format using the provided repack script:

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    python python/sglang/multimodal_gen/tools/wan_repack.py \
      --model-type Wan2.2-T2V-A14B \
      --original-model-path /path/to/Wan2.2-T2V-A14B-Diffusers \
      --quant-path /path/to/wan2_2_mxfp8_weights \
      --output-path /path/to/wan2_2_mxfp8_diffusers
<
Step 3: Run inference

[Command]

[Command]Command

>sh
    sglang generate \
      --model-path /path/to/wan2_2_mxfp8_diffusers \
      --prompt "a beautiful sunset over the mountains" \
      --save-output
<
For pre-quantized checkpoints available on ModelScope, see
modelscope/Eco-Tech https://modelscope.cn/models/Eco-Tech.

- Prompt: `"a cat is playing piano"`

BENCHMARKS           *ascend-npus-optimization-ring_sp_performance-benchmarks*

Benchmark Disclaimer

These numbers are from one fixed setup and one prompt case. Actual
performance may vary by model settings, environment, and workload.

           *ascend-npus-optimization-ring_sp_performance-stage-time-breakdown*
Stage Time Breakdown

Stage / Metric                        u1r2 (s)  u1r1 baseline (s)      Speedup
------------------------------------  --------  ---------------------  -------
InputValidation                       0.0003    0.0002                 0.67x
TextEncoding                          3.5936    3.5820                 1.00x
LatentPreparation                     0.0007    0.0055                 7.86x
TimestepPreparation                   0.0008    0.0007                 0.88x
Denoising                             121.2788  239.2580               1.97x
Decoding                              13.8685   16.4969                1.19x
Total (Pixel data generated)          141.86    266.50                 1.88x

SUMMARY                 *ascend-npus-optimization-ring_sp_performance-summary*

- With `torch_npu==2.10.0`, Ring-SP (`u1r2`) runs successfully on NPU for
  this case.
- End-to-end generation time improves from `266.50s` to `141.86s` (`1.88x`).
- The main gain comes from `DenoisingStage` (`1.97x`), while decoding also
  improves (`1.19x`).

   *ascend-npus-reference-environment_variables-kimi-k3-speculative-attention*
Kimi-K3 speculative attention

Use these switches to optimize DSPARK target verification and draft
attention on Ascend NPUs. Install a version of `sgl-kernel-npu` that exports
`flash_mla`, `flash_mla_metadata`, and `paged_mtp_attention_decode` from
`sgl_kernel_npu.operators.attention` for your NPU. Set the variables in the
server environment on every rank before launching with
`--speculative-algorithm DSPARK`:

>sh
    export SGLANG_NPU_USE_FLASH_MLA=1
    export ASCEND_USE_PAGED_MTP=1
<
You can enable either kernel independently. To also avoid CPU
sequence-length mirror and host attention-parameter updates in these
speculative paths, enable both kernels and set
`SGLANG_NPU_ATTN_BACKEND_NEEDS_CPU_SEQ_LENS=0`. Its default is `1`; the two
kernel switches alone do not disable CPU mirrors. Setting either kernel
switch to `0` keeps the existing attention path for that worker. The
DeepSeek-V4 NPU attention backend also honors this switch for DFlash-family
speculative decoding (dFlash/DSpark verify) without the kernel switches
above, deriving all attention metadata from the device-side `seq_lens`
instead.
